claims.claim: For existentialists, no moral absolute, divine will or natural law can guide or justify our choice
claims.evidence: SEP existentialism §4 Freedom: "There is no moral absolute, divine will, or natural law that can provide guidance or justify our actions."

claims.claim: We alone are responsible
claims.evidence: SEP existentialism §4 Freedom: "we realize that we alone are responsible for our choices and the projects we undertake"

claims.claim: Realising that often brings anxiety
claims.evidence: SEP existentialism §4 Freedom: "the awareness is often accompanied by anxiety because we realize that we alone are responsible" (source ties anxiety to awareness of freedom; equivalent)

claims.claim: Sartre: 'there are no excuses behind us nor justifications before us'
claims.evidence: SEP existentialism §4 Freedom: "condemned to be free because 'there are no excuses behind us nor justifications before us' (Sartre 1946 [2001, 296])"

attribution.evidence: Exercise introduced with "One way to use his point:"; grounded in "you have selected that priest; and at bottom you already knew, more or less, what he would advise." Sartre proposes no exercise; the text does not claim he does.

claims.claim: Sartre's own example is a student
claims.evidence: "the case of a pupil of mine, who sought me out"

claims.claim: Torn between joining the Free French Forces in England and staying with his mother
claims.evidence: "the choice between going to England to join the Free French Forces or of staying near his mother and helping her to live"

claims.claim: His mother lived only for him
claims.evidence: "He fully realised that this woman lived only for him"

claims.claim: The student came to Sartre for advice
claims.evidence: "the youth did, at least, go to a professor to ask for advice"; "in coming to me"

claims.claim: Choosing an adviser, Sartre said, is already a choice
claims.evidence: "to choose an adviser is nevertheless to commit oneself by that choice"

claims.claim: You more or less know what they will say
claims.evidence: "at bottom you already knew, more or less, what he would advise"; "he knew what advice I should give him"

claims.claim: His only reply was 'You are free, therefore choose, that is to say, invent.'
claims.evidence: "I had but one reply to make. You are free, therefore choose, that is to say, invent."

claims.claim: Application: before a hard choice, ask why you picked this adviser and what you expect them to say
claims.evidence: Labelled bridge; consistent with "you have selected that priest ... he would have decided beforehand the kind of advice he was to receive"

items.quote_check: 4/4 quotes verbatim (sep-existentialism.txt §5.5; research-vos-2015 Results, Conclusion x2)

claims.claim: For Sartre and Beauvoir, no fixed meaning is handed to us
claims.evidence: SEP §5.5: "My projects have meaning and value because I chose these projects, but the meaning is contingent; it is never enduring or stable."

claims.claim: Beauvoir said existence is not absurd but ambiguous
claims.evidence: SEP §5.5: "The notion of ambiguity must not be confused with that of absurdity ... to say that it is ambiguous is to assert that its meaning is never fixed"

claims.claim: 'its meaning is never fixed'
claims.evidence: SEP §5.5, verbatim

claims.claim: A 2015 meta-analysis found large effects of meaning therapies on meaning in life
claims.evidence: Vos 2015 Results: "Meaning therapies (n = 6 studies) showed large effects on positive meaning in life immediately postintervention (d = 0.65)"

claims.claim: With particular support for structured ones [meaning therapies] with physically ill patients
claims.evidence: Vos 2015 Conclusion: "We found particular support for structured interventions incorporating psychoeducation, exercises, and discussing meaning in life directly and positively with physically ill patients." The source says 'structured interventions' across existential therapies, not 'structured meaning therapies'; 'ones' narrows the referent to meaning therapies and drops what made them structured. Minor.

claims.claim: The studies were few and low in quality
claims.evidence: Vos 2015 Conclusion: "Despite the small number and low quality of studies"

claims.claim: That is evidence for therapy, not for reflecting alone
claims.evidence: Vos 2015 Results/Conclusion describe RCTs of therapies and 'structured interventions'; nothing on self-guided reflection. Correct caveat.

attribution.evidence: "In therapy, logotherapists often use Socratic questions ..." then "One way to borrow that on your own:" clearly separates the clinical method from the self-exercise. Sources propose no self-exercise.

claims.claim: Frankl was a psychiatrist
claims.evidence: VFI 'What is Logotherapy': "the psychiatrist and neurologist Viktor Emil Frankl"

claims.claim: Frankl held that we discover meaning rather than make it
claims.evidence: VFIL 'Meaning': "we can discover meaning but we can't make meaning"

claims.claim: We should not ask what life means, but recognise 'that it is he who is asked'
claims.evidence: VFIL 'Life has ultimate meaning': "man should not ask what the meaning of his life is, but rather must recognize that it is he who is asked"

claims.claim: The Viktor Frankl Institute of Logotherapy names three avenues to meaning
claims.evidence: VFIL 'Three avenues': "He called these the creative, experiential and attitudinal avenues to meaning-discovery." (institute reports Frankl's scheme)

claims.claim: What we give, through work or deeds
claims.evidence: "Creative actions. Giving of ourselves and contributing to life through meaningful work, deeds, or achieving meaningful goals."

claims.claim: What we receive, through experiences or relationships
claims.evidence: "Experiences. Receiving from life through meaningful experiences or relationships."

claims.claim: The stance we take, especially to suffering we cannot avoid
claims.evidence: "Attitudes. Adopting the right attitude to situations, especially those of unavoidable suffering."

claims.claim: In therapy, logotherapists often use Socratic questions
claims.evidence: VFI 'Socratic dialogue': "Socratic dialogue is a conversational method frequently used by logotherapists. Specific questions are aimed to raise into consciousness ..."

claims.claim: They guide clients towards meanings they find themselves
claims.evidence: VFI 'Will to Meaning': "they are not offered specific meanings. Rather, they are guided and assisted in the realization of those meaning possibilities they have detected themselves."

claims.claim: Application: this week ask what you gave, received, and what stance you took to something you could not change
claims.evidence: Labelled bridge mapping 1:1 onto the three avenues in VFIL

claims.claim: For Nietzsche, the key to living with style is radical acceptance
claims.evidence: SEP §5.3: "The key to living with style is, for Nietzsche, a radical acceptance of one's existence and the world as it is"

claims.claim: Saying yes to your whole life, its strengths and weaknesses, its blessings and curses
claims.evidence: SEP §5.3: "embracing all our strengths and weaknesses and all the blessed and cursed events"; "a 'yes-sayer' who affirms every aspect of his life"

claims.claim: Out of amor fati, a love of one's fate
claims.evidence: SEP §5.3: "overflowing with amor fati (love of one's fate), the Overman welcomes this possibility" (source attaches amor fati to the Overman's welcoming of recurrence, which is the acceptance; acceptable)

claims.claim: He thought only 'the highest types' could manage it [radical acceptance]
claims.evidence: SEP §5.3: "not everyone has the inborn power to rebel against tradition and creatively express their unique style of living. For Nietzsche, only 'the highest types' can manifest this kind of freedom and capacity for self-overcoming." The source's referent is freedom/self-overcoming/creative style; the text re-points 'it' to radical acceptance specifically. Close but sharpened.

attribution.evidence: The demon thought experiment is Nietzsche's own, addressed to the reader ("What if a demon crept after thee ...") so posing it is 'proposed'. The single-day version is the app's adaptation, signalled only by "A smaller start:" with no 'one way to use' framing as in the other two cards; together with the card title 'Would you live this day again?' and from: 'The Gay Science §341', a reader could take the day version as Nietzsche's. Not misattributed, but the weakest label of the three.

claims.claim: A demon tells you you must live this life again, 'innumerable times', with nothing new in it
claims.evidence: GS 341: "thou must live it once more, and also innumerable times; and there will be nothing new in it"

claims.claim: Would you curse the demon, or answer that you never heard anything more divine?
claims.evidence: GS 341: "curse the demon that so spake? Or hast thou once experienced a tremendous moment in which thou wouldst answer him: 'Thou art a God, and never did I hear aught more divine!'" (drops the 'tremendous moment' condition; acceptable simplification)

claims.claim: If the thought took hold of you it would transform you, or perhaps crush you
claims.evidence: GS 341: "If that thought acquired power over thee, as thou art, it would transform thee, and perhaps crush thee"

claims.claim: The question 'Dost thou want this once more?' would lie as the heaviest burden on everything you do
claims.evidence: GS 341: "the question with regard to all and everything: 'Dost thou want this once more, and also for innumerable times?' would lie as the heaviest burden upon thy activity!" The in-text quotation is truncated and re-punctuated without an ellipsis, dropping 'and also for innumerable times', the eternity element; paraphrase of the rest is fine.

claims.claim: One influential reading treats it as a test of whether your life has been good
claims.evidence: SEP Nietzsche §6.3: "an influential line of readings has argued that the thought ... was ... a practical thought experiment designed to test whether one's life has been good" (the text omits the Loeb cosmological pushback; acceptable given 'one reading')

claims.claim: A smaller start: try it on a single day
claims.evidence: Not in either cited section. SEP §6.3 stresses the opposite scope: "if the question is about the value of our life overall", "direct an evaluative judgment onto our life as a whole", and sameness "in every detail" to block elisions. Presenting a one-day version as a 'smaller start' on the same test reframes it; acceptable only as a clearly labelled adaptation.

evidence_risk: practices[1].idea: the Vos 2015 meta-analysis is explicitly caveated ('evidence for therapy, not for reflecting alone'), so it is not presented as support for the self-exercise. Residual risk: the card's from-line is 'Viktor Frankl, logotherapy' but the abstract never names logotherapy (it pools 'meaning therapies', n=6); a reader may take the effect sizes as evidence for logotherapy specifically. No other evidence claims in the graded items.
quotes: 17/17 `quote` fields found verbatim, each exactly once, and every cited section label exists in its source file.
